state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Great job recognizing that the function \( f(x - a) \) involves a translation! Remember, when we have \( f(x - a) \), the graph shifts to the right by \( a \) units, not up. Think about how this affects the x-values and adjust your translation accordingly. Keep up the good work!

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so it's a horizontal shift, not vertical? So if it's f(x - 3), the graph moves to the right by 3 units instead? But I'm still a bit confused about why it goes right when we're subtracting 3 – wouldn't subtracting make it go left?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track! It can be a bit counterintuitive, but when we subtract a value inside the parentheses, it actually shifts the graph to the right. Think about it in terms of the x-values and how they change with the subtraction. Can you try visualizing it on a number line to see why subtracting moves the graph to the right?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Hmm, okay so like... if I think about it on a number line, to get the same y-value I'd need a bigger x-value now, right? So like if f(3) used to give me some answer, now I'd need f(x - 3) = f(3) which means x would have to be 6? Is that why it shifts right – because the x-values have to be bigger to get the same output?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher correctly addresses the vertical-vs-horizontal confusion and prompts reasoning rather than just telling, though the scaffolding could be more targeted; the student demonstrates excellent progress from believing the shift is vertical-upward to independently constructing the correct reasoning about why subtraction causes rightward movement.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher exemplifies the constructive strategy by breaking down the transformation concept into manageable steps, scaffolding from recognizing the type of transformation to understanding the direction, and adjusting support by prompting visualization when the student expresses confusion about the counterintuitive nature of the shift.
